lines: Hey, it's Sam.
I want to tell you why I got into fitness.
I didn't start to look perfect.

cases.name: Q05 suggest, very long topic
cases.input: Why I think that the way most people approach their morning routines, especially those who work long shifts in hospitals and warehouses, is setting them up to fail before the day even begins
lines: Hey, it's Sam.
I want to talk about morning routines.
Most people wake up, scroll their phone, chug coffee, and rush out the door.
If you work long shifts in a hospital or warehouse, that start drains you before your day even begins.
I see it in fitness all the time.
Your morning should give you energy, not steal it.
Let's change that together.

cases.name: Q06 suggest, special characters
cases.input: C++ vs. Rust: <why> & 'how' — 100%?
lines: Hey, it's Sam.
If I had to pick between C++ and Rust, I'd pick Rust.
C++ is powerful, but Rust feels safer for me.
Why?
Because it catches mistakes before they become bugs.
That means less time fixing crashes and more time building.
I'm still learning, but that's why I'm here.
If I stumble, I smile and keep going.
Let's build something together.

cases.name: Q07 suggest, pro level 60s hot take
cases.input: Your hot take about tech
lines: Hey, it's Sam.
As someone who talks about tech every day, my hot take is this: the best tech is the tech you don't notice.
Reason one: when something works perfectly, it gets out of your way and lets you focus on what actually matters.
Reason two: the more you notice your tools, the more they feel like chores instead of help.
Think about the apps you love most.
You probably don't think about the code or the servers.
You just use them.
So I think we should design for invisibility, not for flashy features.
Now, I know plenty of people love seeing every bell and whistle.
I'd love to hear why you disagree.
Drop your take in the comments.

cases.name: Q11 suggest, story day, minimal profile (fabrication check)
cases.input: The day something went wrong
lines: I thought I was ready to cook for a friend.
I wasn't.
I wanted to make [dish] at my place, but I forgot to set a timer.
Smoke filled the kitchen, and the [dish] came out charcoal.
We ordered pizza and laughed instead.
We still ate well, just not what I planned.
Some days, the best part isn't the food—it's the friend you're with when everything burns.

cases.name: P05 polish, long draft (~280 words) at 30s
cases.input: So basically I started my fitness journey back in March 2021 when my doctor, Dr. Patel, told me my blood pressure was 150 over 95 which honestly scared me a lot. I was working as an accountant in Manchester and sitting at my desk for like ten hours a day and I never moved. At first I just walked 5,000 steps every day and then I slowly moved up to 10,000 steps and I started going to the gym three times a week on Monday Wednesday and Friday. My friend Jordan came with me and he showed me how to deadlift properly because I was doing it completely wrong and I hurt my back once. After about eight months I lost 14 kilos and my blood pressure went down to 120 over 80 which my doctor was really happy about. Now I make videos for people who work desk jobs because I think most fitness content is made for people who already love the gym and that's not most people. I really believe you don't need two hours a day, you need twenty minutes and consistency, and I want to show that it's possible even if you hate exercise like I did. Anyway yeah that's kind of my story and why I do this.
lines: In March 2021, my doctor told me my blood pressure was 150 over 95.
That scared me.
I was an accountant, sitting ten hours a day.
I started with 5,000 steps, then 10,000, then the gym three times a week.
After eight months, I lost 14 kilos and my blood pressure came down.
Now I make videos for desk workers.
You don't need two hours a day.
You need twenty minutes and consistency.
